requirements.product_understanding: A backend system that supports real-time multiplayer battle-royale games with 100 players per match, using an authoritative server model where the server validates all game actions to prevent cheating. The system must provide sub-100ms perceived input latency to ensure responsive gameplay for players worldwide.
users_and_use_cases: Players (mobile + PC) - join matches, send input commands, receive game state updates, experience seamless gameplay with low latency
Game studio ops - monitor match performance, track system health, manage server resources, troubleshoot issues during live matches
functional: Support 100 concurrent players per match with authoritative server simulation
Process and validate all player inputs on the server to prevent cheating
Maintain sub-100ms perceived input latency for all players worldwide
Handle 50,000 concurrent matches at peak traffic
Provide real-time game state synchronization to all players in a match
Support global distribution with low-latency connections for worldwide players
non_functional: Total monthly operational budget limited to $80,000
Server-authoritative model must be enforced with no client-side trust
Input latency must remain under 100ms for all players regardless of geographic location
assumptions: The game studio will provide detailed technical specifications for the authoritative server model and input validation requirements
All players will have internet connectivity sufficient to maintain the required latency targets
The system will be deployed in a cloud environment with global edge locations to support worldwide low-latency connections
Match duration and game state complexity are within expected parameters for the specified latency requirements
open_questions: What specific input types and frequencies need to be processed to maintain the sub-100ms latency requirement?
How will the system handle network partitioning or connectivity issues during matches?
What is the expected match duration distribution to properly size server resources?
Will there be any dedicated infrastructure requirements for the authoritative server model beyond standard compute and networking?
What level of monitoring and alerting capabilities are required for game studio operations?

components.name: Matchmaking Service
components.description: Responsible for creating and managing game sessions, assigning players to matches, and handling match lifecycle events including start, end, and player join/leave operations. This service ensures that each match maintains exactly 100 players and coordinates with the Game Simulation Engine to begin simulation when all players are ready. It also handles match state transitions and communicates with the Load Balancer for optimal server placement based on geographic proximity to players. The service is designed as a purely stateful component, using direct database access for match metadata management with simple transactions instead of caching or consensus protocols.

components.name: Game Simulation Engine
components.description: The core authoritative server component that runs the game simulation logic for each active match. It processes all player inputs in real-time, validates them against game rules, updates game state, and broadcasts synchronized updates to all players in the match. This engine is designed to handle 100 concurrent players per match with sub-100ms latency requirements through a lock-based architecture that allows parallel processing of inputs within a single match while maintaining strict sequential consistency. It implements a direct input processing pipeline without message brokers, using actor model for asynchronous input processing before synchronization in the game state.

components.name: Global Load Balancer
components.description: Distributes incoming match requests to the most appropriate regional game servers based on player geographic location and current server load. This component ensures that players are routed to servers with minimal latency while balancing load across available resources. It continuously monitors server health, performance metrics, and geographic distribution to make optimal routing decisions for new matches and handle dynamic scaling requirements. The system uses a multi-tiered connection management approach with separate WebSocket gateways per region.

components.name: Real-Time Communication Layer
components.description: Provides persistent bidirectional communication channels between players and the Game Simulation Engine using WebSocket connections for low-latency data transmission. This layer handles input command streaming from players, real-time game state updates, and ensures reliable delivery of critical game events. It implements connection pooling, automatic reconnection logic, bandwidth optimization techniques, and circuit breaker patterns to prevent cascading failures. Player inputs are streamed directly to the Game Simulation Engine via WebSocket connections without queuing through message brokers.

components.name: Match State Persistence
components.description: Maintains historical match data for post-match analysis, replay generation, and operational insights. This component stores match metadata, player performance statistics, and game event logs in a distributed database system optimized for both write-heavy operations during matches and read-heavy operations for analytics. Input command payloads are encrypted at rest using customer-managed keys.

components.name: Monitoring & Operations Dashboard
components.description: Provides real-time visibility into system health, performance metrics, and operational status for game studio operations. This component aggregates data from all other services to display match statistics, server utilization, latency trends, and alerting information for operational decision-making. It includes dynamic threshold adjustment using machine learning models trained on historical traffic data.

architecture.infrastructure: Cloud-based global infrastructure with edge locations in major regions. Each region contains dedicated compute clusters running the Game Simulation Engine and Real-Time Communication Layer components. The system uses auto-scaling groups to dynamically adjust server capacity based on match demand while maintaining strict regional distribution for latency optimization. Network infrastructure includes content delivery networks (CDNs), direct peering connections, and AWS PrivateLink for secure service access. Micro-segmentation using VPC Security Groups and Network ACLs isolates match data by region and game type.

decisions.alternatives_considered: HTTP/2 streaming, gRPC streaming, UDP with custom reliability layer
decisions.trade_offs: WebSocket provides persistent connection with built-in message ordering and reliability features while maintaining compatibility with standard web infrastructure
decisions.rationale: The requirement for sub-100ms perceived input latency necessitates a persistent connection model that can handle tens of updates per second per user. WebSocket supports bidirectional communication with minimal overhead, enabling the system to maintain low-latency connections without requiring complex custom protocols.

decisions.decision: Implement lock-based architecture in Game Simulation Engine
decisions.alternatives_considered: Traditional mutex-based synchronization, actor model, read-write locks, hybrid approach
decisions.trade_offs: Lock-based approach provides simpler implementation and better performance under high concurrency for 100-player matches
decisions.rationale: With 100 players per match and potentially thousands of concurrent matches, the simulation engine must process inputs at extremely high rates while maintaining deterministic behavior. The lock-based approach is simpler to implement and maintain than the hybrid approach, and provides sufficient performance for the specified requirements.

decisions.decision: Deploy regional server clusters with global load balancing
decisions.alternatives_considered: Single global cluster, centralized processing, hybrid cloud approach
decisions.trade_offs: Regional deployment increases operational complexity but reduces latency for players worldwide
decisions.rationale: The sub-100ms latency requirement cannot be met with a single centralized server. Geographic distribution using regional clusters ensures that players connect to servers within their network proximity while maintaining overall system scalability and cost efficiency.

decisions.alternatives_considered: Stateless matchmaker, distributed consensus protocols, event sourcing, hybrid approach
decisions.trade_offs: Purely stateful approach reduces complexity and eliminates potential consistency issues
decisions.rationale: The system must support 50,000 concurrent matches at peak traffic while maintaining 99.95% availability. A purely stateful approach using direct database access provides the necessary simplicity and reliability without introducing single points of failure or complex caching layers.

security_controls.threat_model_summary: Primary threats include: (1) Cheating through input manipulation or client-side tampering, mitigated by authoritative server model with lock-free input validation; (2) DDoS attacks targeting matchmaking or input endpoints, addressed via rate limiting and API gateway protection; (3) Geographic latency degradation affecting gameplay, countered by regional server clusters; (4) Data corruption in match state persistence, handled through distributed database replication; (5) Operational dashboard compromise leading to match disruption, protected by least-privilege access controls.
security_controls.authentication: OAuth2 with short-lived JWTs validated at the API Gateway for all administrative endpoints. Player authentication handled via game studio's existing identity provider using OAuth2 flows with refresh token rotation. No client-side trust in player inputs - all validation occurs server-side in Game Simulation Engine. Token validation cache with TTL-based invalidation implemented at API Gateway level. Session management layer maintains an in-memory cache of active player sessions with short TTLs (15-30 minutes) and integrates with identity provider's token revocation API for immediate invalidation upon logout or security events.
security_controls.authorization: Role-based access control (RBAC) at API Gateway level with predefined roles: 'matchmaker', 'game-engine', 'ops-dashboard', and 'player'. Matchmaking Service and Game Simulation Engine use service-to-service JWTs with audience validation. Operations Dashboard has read-only access to match state, write access only for emergency match termination. Mutual TLS (mTLS) with certificate pinning enforced for all inter-service communication. Service-level authorization policies using mTLS, JWT audience validation, and internal API gateways enforce role-based permissions for cross-service calls. Request context validation within each service prevents unauthorized access even if mTLS is bypassed.
security_controls.iam: Service accounts with least-privilege permissions for each component. Matchmaking Service uses AWS IAM roles with specific S3 and DynamoDB permissions for match state management. Game Simulation Engine uses dedicated service accounts with minimal required permissions. All inter-service communication uses mutual TLS (mTLS) with certificate-based authentication.
security_controls.network_boundaries: All internal components communicate via private VPC networks with security groups enforcing strict egress/ingress rules. API Gateway sits in public subnet with WAF protection and rate limiting. Regional server clusters are isolated by VPC peering connections. Matchmaking Service uses DynamoDB Global Tables for cross-region consistency with read replicas in each region. Micro-segmentation using AWS VPC Security Groups and Network ACLs isolates match data by region and game type. Strict inter-region VPC peering rules with minimal allowed protocols and ports enforced. AWS Transit Gateway used for centralized routing and monitoring of cross-region traffic. Deep packet inspection (DPI) or network behavior analytics implemented to detect anomalous traffic patterns between regions.
security_controls.secrets_and_encryption: All secrets managed via AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation. TLS certificates stored in AWS Certificate Manager with automatic renewal. Data at rest encrypted using AWS KMS with customer-managed keys. All inter-service communication uses mTLS with certificate pinning. Input commands are encrypted in transit and validated server-side using HMAC signatures to prevent replay attacks. Input command payloads stored in databases or logs are also encrypted at rest using customer-managed keys. Automated key rotation for customer-managed KMS keys used for encrypting input payloads, with audit trail logging of all encryption/decryption operations. Time-based validation (TTL) added to nonces in addition to sequence numbers, and centralized event store with cryptographic signatures implemented to track and validate command order across time windows.

reliability_design.scaling_strategy: The Game Simulation Engine is the primary scaling bottleneck due to its lock-free architecture requiring high-performance compute per match. Scaling is achieved through regional server clusters with auto-scaling groups that dynamically adjust based on concurrent match count and player load. Each region maintains capacity for ~5,000 matches (100 players each) to ensure sub-100ms latency. The Global Load Balancer distributes new matches to underutilized regions, while the Matchmaking Service uses direct database access for match metadata management.
reliability_design.reliability: The system targets 99.95% availability with RTO of 30 seconds for service recovery and RPO of 1 second for match state data. The Matchmaking Service uses a purely stateful approach with direct database access for match metadata, while the Game Simulation Engine implements asynchronous background checkpointing with dedicated storage layer for match state snapshots. Regional redundancy is achieved through cross-region replication of critical match metadata with automatic failover to healthy regions within 30 seconds.
reliability_design.disaster_recovery: Cross-region failover is implemented for the Game Simulation Engine clusters using active-passive configuration with automated failover triggered by regional health monitoring. Matchmaking state is replicated across two regions with 1-second sync latency. In case of region-wide outages, the system automatically redirects new matches to healthy regions while maintaining existing match continuity through state synchronization protocols. Recovery time for complete region failure is 2 minutes with full service restoration. Multi-tiered backup strategy includes regular snapshot-based backups, real-time replication of critical match metadata, and defined recovery playbook. Match state snapshots stored in geographically distributed S3 buckets with versioning enabled for quick restoration.
reliability_design.observability: Comprehensive monitoring includes real-time latency metrics (p99 < 50ms), match state sync delays, and server load indicators via Prometheus/Grafana dashboards. Key performance indicators include: input processing rate (10k+ commands/sec per match), game tick duration (< 16ms for 100 players), and connection drop rates (< 0.01%). Alerting thresholds are set at 200ms latency for p95, 500ms for p99, and immediate alerts for any service unavailability or region failures. Dynamic threshold adjustment using machine learning models trained on historical traffic data. Specific monitoring added for input command processing rates with alerting thresholds set at 80% and 95% utilization, including metrics for queue depth, processing latency per command type, and error rates.
failure_scenarios: Matchmaking Service node failure: Automatic failover to healthy nodes within 30 seconds using direct database access with transactional integrity. New matches are queued until service restores, with existing matches continuing unaffected.

Game Simulation Engine cluster crash: Regional failover occurs within 2 minutes with automatic resynchronization of match state from last checkpoint. Players experience < 100ms disruption during failover process.

Network partition between region and players: Real-Time Communication Layer implements automatic reconnection logic with retry mechanisms. Connection timeouts are set to 5 seconds with fallback to nearest available regional server.

Input command queue overflow: The Game Simulation Engine uses bounded queues with priority-based processing for critical inputs (movement, shooting). Overflow handling triggers immediate latency alerts but maintains game state integrity through sequence number validation and nonce-based replay prevention.

Global Load Balancer failure: Regional load balancers continue operation with local match distribution. Global routing is restored within 1 minute with minimal impact to new match creation and existing match continuity.

Cascading failures in Real-Time Communication Layer: Circuit breaker patterns and connection throttling mechanisms prevent cascading failures. Connection pooling with automatic reconnection logic includes exponential backoff and jitter to reduce load on downstream systems during high-traffic or failure scenarios.

findings.issue: Player authentication relies on game studio's external identity provider with refresh token rotation, but no mechanism is defined to handle token revocation or immediate invalidation upon logout or security events in the real-time communication layer.
findings.recommendation: Implement a centralized session management service that maintains an in-memory cache of active player sessions with short TTLs (15-30 minutes) and integrates with the identity provider's token revocation API for immediate invalidation upon logout or security events. This ensures that even if a player's tokens are compromised, they cannot continue to access the system without valid, unrevoked credentials.

findings.issue: While mutual TLS (mTLS) and JWT audience validation are implemented for inter-service communication, there is no defined mechanism to enforce least-privilege access control at the API gateway level for player-facing endpoints.
findings.recommendation: Define granular RBAC policies at the API gateway level for all player-facing endpoints, ensuring that each endpoint only allows access based on specific roles and permissions. For example, the /players/{player_id}/input endpoint should be restricted to authenticated players with valid session tokens, and not allow arbitrary access from any client.

findings.issue: The architecture specifies micro-segmentation using VPC Security Groups and Network ACLs, but does not define how network traffic between regional clusters will be monitored or protected against lateral movement in case of a breach.
findings.recommendation: Implement deep packet inspection (DPI) or network behavior analytics to monitor cross-region traffic for anomalous patterns. Additionally, configure strict inter-region VPC peering rules with minimal allowed protocols and ports enforced, and establish a centralized logging system to track all inter-service communication for potential security incidents.

findings.issue: Input command payloads are encrypted at rest using customer-managed keys, but there is no defined mechanism to rotate these keys or audit encryption/decryption operations in case of a security incident.
findings.recommendation: Establish an automated key rotation schedule for customer-managed KMS keys used for encrypting input payloads, and implement comprehensive logging of all encryption/decryption operations with audit trails. This ensures that even if a key is compromised, the system can quickly rotate to a new key and trace any unauthorized access attempts.

findings.issue: The Game Simulation Engine directly streams input commands from players via WebSocket connections without implementing any rate limiting or anomaly detection on input command frequency or size, which could lead to resource exhaustion or DoS attacks.
findings.recommendation: Implement rate limiting and anomaly detection at the Real-Time Communication Layer level to monitor input command frequency and size. Set thresholds for maximum commands per second per player and alert on unusual spikes. Additionally, validate all input payloads server-side using HMAC signatures to prevent replay attacks and ensure integrity of commands before processing them in the Game Simulation Engine.

findings.issue: The system requires substantial compute resources for 50,000 concurrent matches with 100 players each. The Game Simulation Engine's lock-based architecture demands high-performance CPUs to process inputs at scale, and global distribution across multiple regions increases networking costs significantly.
findings.recommendation: The estimate assumes 5,000 matches per region with regional clusters; this is a tight margin for scaling without additional compute resources. Consider adding buffer capacity or exploring more cost-efficient instance types if budget constraints are tight.

findings.issue: WebSocket connections for 50,000 concurrent matches (100 players each) require significant infrastructure to maintain low-latency persistent connections. The system must support ~5M concurrent WebSocket connections with minimal overhead.
findings.recommendation: This component is likely underpriced in the current estimate. The cost of maintaining millions of persistent connections, especially across global regions, can quickly escalate beyond budget if not carefully managed.

findings.issue: The purely stateful approach using direct database access for 50,000 matches is expensive and may hit database throughput limits. DynamoDB or similar services will be heavily utilized, especially during peak match creation times.
findings.recommendation: While the system avoids caching and consensus protocols, it relies on direct DB transactions which could become a bottleneck. Ensure sufficient provisioned capacity for DynamoDB to avoid performance degradation.

findings.issue: The dashboard uses machine learning models for dynamic threshold adjustment, which may require additional compute resources and potentially increase costs beyond the baseline estimate.
findings.recommendation: ML-based alerting adds complexity and cost. Verify that this component's resource usage is accurately reflected in the estimate.

findings.issue: The system implements mutual TLS, certificate pinning, and encryption at rest with customer-managed keys, which are all standard but add overhead in terms of infrastructure and operational costs.
findings.recommendation: Ensure that security controls do not introduce unexpected scaling or performance bottlenecks. These features should be included in the estimate but may require additional budget if they're not already factored in.

findings.issue: The Matchmaking Service is designed as a purely stateful component using direct database access, but no explicit redundancy or failover mechanism is defined for the database layer itself. If the primary database instance fails, all matchmaking operations would halt until recovery.
findings.recommendation: Implement multi-AZ deployment with automatic failover for the Matchmaking Service's database layer (e.g., DynamoDB Global Tables or RDS Multi-AZ). Ensure that match state metadata can be replicated across regions with <1s sync latency to maintain 99.95% availability target.

findings.issue: The system's reliability design specifies an RTO of 30 seconds for service recovery and RPO of 1 second for match state data. However, the Game Simulation Engine uses lock-based architecture which may not scale efficiently under high load, potentially leading to latency spikes that could push the system below the required 99.95% availability threshold during peak traffic.
findings.recommendation: Conduct performance stress testing at 50,000 concurrent matches to validate that the lock-based simulation engine maintains sub-100ms latency under all conditions. If performance degrades beyond acceptable thresholds, consider implementing a hybrid synchronization model (e.g., lock-free data structures with optimistic concurrency control) to ensure consistent low-latency behavior.

findings.issue: While the system mentions snapshot-based backups and real-time replication of critical match metadata, there is no defined recovery playbook or automated restore process for full regional failures. The disaster recovery plan relies on manual intervention steps that may not meet the 2-minute RTO requirement during complete region outages.
findings.recommendation: Develop and automate a comprehensive recovery playbook with predefined scripts and procedures for restoring match state from backups within 2 minutes. Implement automated failover mechanisms using Route53 health checks or similar tools to ensure seamless redirection of traffic to healthy regions during regional failures.

findings.issue: The failure scenario analysis does not account for potential cascading failures in the Real-Time Communication Layer due to connection pooling exhaustion or circuit breaker triggers. These could lead to widespread disconnections and affect match continuity even if underlying systems are healthy.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit monitoring and alerting for connection pool utilization, circuit breaker state transitions, and retry rates in the Real-Time Communication Layer. Implement adaptive connection pooling with dynamic scaling based on current load to prevent resource exhaustion during traffic spikes.

findings.issue: Monitoring includes latency metrics and match state sync delays but lacks visibility into input command processing rate variations across different command types (e.g., movement vs. shooting). This could mask performance bottlenecks specific to certain input categories.
findings.recommendation: Enhance observability by adding granular metrics for each input command type with separate alerting thresholds. Include metrics such as average processing time per command type, queue depth per command category, and error rates broken down by command type to enable targeted optimization.

findings.issue: The architecture relies on REST POST endpoints for player input commands (POST /players/{player_id}/input) which is fundamentally incompatible with real-time, high-frequency requirements. With 100 players per match and potentially thousands of concurrent matches, this creates a massive scaling bottleneck where each input command must be serialized through an HTTP request/response cycle, introducing unnecessary latency and serialization overhead.
findings.recommendation: Replace REST POST endpoints with WebSocket streams or gRPC streaming for player inputs. The current approach will cause input latency to exceed 100ms even under ideal conditions due to HTTP overhead, connection establishment delays, and queuing in the API gateway layer. This is a critical architectural flaw that will prevent meeting the sub-100ms requirement at scale.

findings.issue: The purely stateful matchmaking service using direct database access for all match metadata operations creates a single point of failure and scalability bottleneck. With 50,000 concurrent matches, this service will become overwhelmed by transactional overhead and database contention, especially when handling player join/leave events and match lifecycle transitions.
findings.recommendation: Implement a hybrid stateful/stateless approach with Redis-based caching for frequently accessed match metadata. Use eventual consistency patterns for non-critical match state updates while maintaining critical transactional integrity in DynamoDB. Introduce match state sharding based on geographic regions to distribute load and reduce database contention.

findings.issue: The lock-based architecture approach is a fundamental flaw that will create severe performance bottlenecks at scale. With 100 players per match, the engine must process thousands of inputs per second while maintaining strict sequential consistency within each match. Lock contention and thread synchronization overhead will cause input latency to exceed 100ms even with optimized code.
findings.recommendation: Replace lock-based architecture with a lock-free, actor-based approach or use concurrent data structures like ReadWriteLocks with proper partitioning. Implement a multi-threaded simulation engine where each match is processed by dedicated threads, and use message queues for inter-match coordination to avoid global locks that will become performance bottlenecks at 50,000 concurrent matches.

findings.issue: The Matchmaking Service and Game Simulation Engine both handle match state management with overlapping responsibilities. The Matchmaking Service maintains match metadata in the database while the Game Simulation Engine also needs to track match state for simulation, creating duplicated logic and potential consistency issues.
findings.recommendation: Consolidate match state management into a single authoritative source (likely the Game Simulation Engine) with the Matchmaking Service acting purely as a coordinator that routes players to appropriate servers. Remove the direct database access from Matchmaking Service and implement a proper event-driven architecture where match lifecycle events are published to a message bus for consumption by other services.

findings.issue: The global load balancer's multi-tiered connection management approach with separate WebSocket gateways per region creates unnecessary complexity and potential failure points. This design doesn't account for dynamic traffic patterns or optimal routing based on real-time network conditions.
findings.recommendation: Implement a more sophisticated load balancing algorithm that considers not just geographic proximity but also real-time network performance metrics, server health, and current match load. Use a centralized load balancer with regional proxies rather than separate gateways to reduce complexity and improve routing efficiency.

findings.issue: The monitoring system's reliance on dynamic threshold adjustment using machine learning models introduces a potential single point of failure and makes the system less predictable. If the ML model fails or produces incorrect thresholds, it could either miss critical issues or generate false alerts.
findings.recommendation: Implement a hybrid alerting system that combines static thresholds with dynamic adjustments. Keep core alerting logic simple and robust while using ML models for anomaly detection rather than primary threshold setting. Add circuit breaker patterns to the monitoring components themselves to prevent cascading failures.

architecture_stages.characteristics: A minimal viable architecture that validates the core multiplayer battle-royale backend with essential features while maintaining the authoritative server model. The system focuses on proving the fundamental gameplay loop with reduced scale and simplified infrastructure.
architecture_stages.purpose: Validate core gameplay mechanics and latency requirements with minimal investment before scaling to full production
architecture_stages.transition_trigger: After 3 months of operation with 1,000 concurrent matches and demonstrated sub-100ms latency under controlled conditions, confirming the basic architecture works for real-time authoritative simulation with 100 players per match

architecture_stages.characteristics: An extension of the MVP that supports full production scale while maintaining the core architectural decisions. The system handles 50,000 concurrent matches at peak traffic with enhanced reliability and monitoring capabilities.
architecture_stages.purpose: Scale to full production capacity with robust operational support and performance optimizations
architecture_stages.transition_trigger: When the system reaches 40,000 concurrent matches and begins showing latency spikes above 120ms in 5% of matches during peak hours, indicating need for additional regional capacity or optimization

architecture_stages.characteristics: A fully distributed architecture with specialized services, regional partitioning, and advanced scalability patterns to handle 50,000 concurrent matches while maintaining sub-100ms latency across global players. Includes multi-region failover, specialized game state management, and optimized input processing pipelines.
architecture_stages.purpose: Achieve global scale with enterprise-grade reliability, performance optimization, and operational maturity
architecture_stages.transition_trigger: When the system consistently experiences 250ms+ latency for 1% of players during peak hours or when match state synchronization delays exceed 100ms in 3% of matches, requiring architectural changes to handle global distribution at full scale

security_controls.threat_model_summary: Primary threats include: (1) Cheating through input manipulation or client-side tampering, mitigated by authoritative server model with lock-free input validation; (2) DDoS attacks targeting matchmaking or input endpoints, addressed via rate limiting and API gateway protection; (3) Geographic latency degradation affecting gameplay, countered by regional server clusters; (4) Data corruption in match state persistence, handled through distributed database replication; (5) Operational dashboard compromise leading to match disruption, protected by least-privilege access controls.
security_controls.authentication: OAuth2 with short-lived JWTs validated at the API Gateway for all administrative endpoints. Player authentication handled via game studio's existing identity provider using OAuth2 flows with refresh token rotation. No client-side trust in player inputs - all validation occurs server-side in Game Simulation Engine. Token validation cache with TTL-based invalidation implemented at API Gateway level. Session management layer maintains an in-memory cache of active player sessions with short TTLs (15-30 minutes) and integrates with identity provider's token revocation API for immediate invalidation upon logout or security events.
security_controls.authorization: Role-based access control (RBAC) at API Gateway level with predefined roles: 'matchmaker', 'game-engine', 'ops-dashboard', and 'player'. Matchmaking Service and Game Simulation Engine use service-to-service JWTs with audience validation. Operations Dashboard has read-only access to match state, write access only for emergency match termination. Mutual TLS (mTLS) with certificate pinning enforced for all inter-service communication. Service-level authorization policies using mTLS, JWT audience validation, and internal API gateways enforce role-based permissions for cross-service calls. Request context validation within each service prevents unauthorized access even if mTLS is bypassed.
security_controls.iam: Service accounts with least-privilege permissions for each component. Matchmaking Service uses AWS IAM roles with specific S3 and DynamoDB permissions for match state management. Game Simulation Engine uses dedicated service accounts with minimal required permissions. All inter-service communication uses mutual TLS (mTLS) with certificate-based authentication.
security_controls.network_boundaries: All internal components communicate via private VPC networks with security groups enforcing strict egress/ingress rules. API Gateway sits in public subnet with WAF protection and rate limiting. Regional server clusters are isolated by VPC peering connections. Matchmaking Service uses DynamoDB Global Tables for cross-region consistency with read replicas in each region. Micro-segmentation using AWS VPC Security Groups and Network ACLs isolates match data by region and game type. Strict inter-region VPC peering rules with minimal allowed protocols and ports enforced. AWS Transit Gateway used for centralized routing and monitoring of cross-region traffic. Deep packet inspection (DPI) or network behavior analytics implemented to detect anomalous traffic patterns between regions.
security_controls.secrets_and_encryption: All secrets managed via AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation. TLS certificates stored in AWS Certificate Manager with automatic renewal. Data at rest encrypted using AWS KMS with customer-managed keys. All inter-service communication uses mTLS with certificate pinning. Input commands are encrypted in transit and validated server-side using HMAC signatures to prevent replay attacks. Input command payloads stored in databases or logs are also encrypted at rest using customer-managed keys. Automated key rotation for customer-managed KMS keys used for encrypting input payloads, with audit trail logging of all encryption/decryption operations. Time-based validation (TTL) added to nonces in addition to sequence numbers, and centralized event store with cryptographic signatures implemented to track and validate command order across time windows.

threats.issue: Player authentication relies on game studio's external identity provider with refresh token rotation, but no mechanism is defined to handle token revocation or immediate invalidation upon logout or security events in the real-time communication layer.
threats.recommendation: Implement a centralized session management service that maintains an in-memory cache of active player sessions with short TTLs (15-30 minutes) and integrates with the identity provider's token revocation API for immediate invalidation upon logout or security events. This ensures that even if a player's tokens are compromised, they cannot continue to access the system without valid, unrevoked credentials.

threats.issue: While mutual TLS (mTLS) and JWT audience validation are implemented for inter-service communication, there is no defined mechanism to enforce least-privilege access control at the API gateway level for player-facing endpoints.
threats.recommendation: Define granular RBAC policies at the API gateway level for all player-facing endpoints, ensuring that each endpoint only allows access based on specific roles and permissions. For example, the /players/{player_id}/input endpoint should be restricted to authenticated players with valid session tokens, and not allow arbitrary access from any client.

threats.issue: The architecture specifies micro-segmentation using VPC Security Groups and Network ACLs, but does not define how network traffic between regional clusters will be monitored or protected against lateral movement in case of a breach.
threats.recommendation: Implement deep packet inspection (DPI) or network behavior analytics to monitor cross-region traffic for anomalous patterns. Additionally, configure strict inter-region VPC peering rules with minimal allowed protocols and ports enforced, and establish a centralized logging system to track all inter-service communication for potential security incidents.

threats.issue: Input command payloads are encrypted at rest using customer-managed keys, but there is no defined mechanism to rotate these keys or audit encryption/decryption operations in case of a security incident.
threats.recommendation: Establish an automated key rotation schedule for customer-managed KMS keys used for encrypting input payloads, and implement comprehensive logging of all encryption/decryption operations with audit trails. This ensures that even if a key is compromised, the system can quickly rotate to a new key and trace any unauthorized access attempts.

threats.issue: The Game Simulation Engine directly streams input commands from players via WebSocket connections without implementing any rate limiting or anomaly detection on input command frequency or size, which could lead to resource exhaustion or DoS attacks.
threats.recommendation: Implement rate limiting and anomaly detection at the Real-Time Communication Layer level to monitor input command frequency and size. Set thresholds for maximum commands per second per player and alert on unusual spikes. Additionally, validate all input payloads server-side using HMAC signatures to prevent replay attacks and ensure integrity of commands before processing them in the Game Simulation Engine.

blueprint.infrastructure: Cloud-based global infrastructure with edge locations in major regions. Each region contains dedicated compute clusters running the Game Simulation Engine and Real-Time Communication Layer components. The system uses auto-scaling groups to dynamically adjust server capacity based on match demand while maintaining strict regional distribution for latency optimization. Network infrastructure includes content delivery networks (CDNs), direct peering connections, and AWS PrivateLink for secure service access. Micro-segmentation using VPC Security Groups and Network ACLs isolates match data by region and game type.
blueprint.scaling_strategy: The Game Simulation Engine is the primary scaling bottleneck due to its lock-free architecture requiring high-performance compute per match. Scaling is achieved through regional server clusters with auto-scaling groups that dynamically adjust based on concurrent match count and player load. Each region maintains capacity for ~5,000 matches (100 players each) to ensure sub-100ms latency. The Global Load Balancer distributes new matches to underutilized regions, while the Matchmaking Service uses direct database access for match metadata management.
blueprint.reliability: The system targets 99.95% availability with RTO of 30 seconds for service recovery and RPO of 1 second for match state data. The Matchmaking Service uses a purely stateful approach with direct database access for match metadata, while the Game Simulation Engine implements asynchronous background checkpointing with dedicated storage layer for match state snapshots. Regional redundancy is achieved through cross-region replication of critical match metadata with automatic failover to healthy regions within 30 seconds.
blueprint.disaster_recovery: Cross-region failover is implemented for the Game Simulation Engine clusters using active-passive configuration with automated failover triggered by regional health monitoring. Matchmaking state is replicated across two regions with 1-second sync latency. In case of region-wide outages, the system automatically redirects new matches to healthy regions while maintaining existing match continuity through state synchronization protocols. Recovery time for complete region failure is 2 minutes with full service restoration. Multi-tiered backup strategy includes regular snapshot-based backups, real-time replication of critical match metadata, and defined recovery playbook. Match state snapshots stored in geographically distributed S3 buckets with versioning enabled for quick restoration.
blueprint.observability: Comprehensive monitoring includes real-time latency metrics (p99 < 50ms), match state sync delays, and server load indicators via Prometheus/Grafana dashboards. Key performance indicators include: input processing rate (10k+ commands/sec per match), game tick duration (< 16ms for 100 players), and connection drop rates (< 0.01%). Alerting thresholds are set at 200ms latency for p95, 500ms for p99, and immediate alerts for any service unavailability or region failures. Dynamic threshold adjustment using machine learning models trained on historical traffic data. Specific monitoring added for input command processing rates with alerting thresholds set at 80% and 95% utilization, including metrics for queue depth, processing latency per command type, and error rates.
failure_scenarios: Matchmaking Service node failure: Automatic failover to healthy nodes within 30 seconds using direct database access with transactional integrity. New matches are queued until service restores, with existing matches continuing unaffected.

Game Simulation Engine cluster crash: Regional failover occurs within 2 minutes with automatic resynchronization of match state from last checkpoint. Players experience < 100ms disruption during failover process.

Network partition between region and players: Real-Time Communication Layer implements automatic reconnection logic with retry mechanisms. Connection timeouts are set to 5 seconds with fallback to nearest available regional server.

Input command queue overflow: The Game Simulation Engine uses bounded queues with priority-based processing for critical inputs (movement, shooting). Overflow handling triggers immediate latency alerts but maintains game state integrity through sequence number validation and nonce-based replay prevention.

Global Load Balancer failure: Regional load balancers continue operation with local match distribution. Global routing is restored within 1 minute with minimal impact to new match creation and existing match continuity.

Cascading failures in Real-Time Communication Layer: Circuit breaker patterns and connection throttling mechanisms prevent cascading failures. Connection pooling with automatic reconnection logic includes exponential backoff and jitter to reduce load on downstream systems during high-traffic or failure scenarios.

decisions.alternatives_considered: HTTP/2 streaming, gRPC streaming, UDP with custom reliability layer
decisions.trade_offs: WebSocket provides persistent connection with built-in message ordering and reliability features while maintaining compatibility with standard web infrastructure
decisions.rationale: The requirement for sub-100ms perceived input latency necessitates a persistent connection model that can handle tens of updates per second per user. WebSocket supports bidirectional communication with minimal overhead, enabling the system to maintain low-latency connections without requiring complex custom protocols.

decisions.decision: Implement lock-based architecture in Game Simulation Engine
decisions.alternatives_considered: Traditional mutex-based synchronization, actor model, read-write locks, hybrid approach
decisions.trade_offs: Lock-based approach provides simpler implementation and better performance under high concurrency for 100-player matches
decisions.rationale: With 100 players per match and potentially thousands of concurrent matches, the simulation engine must process inputs at extremely high rates while maintaining deterministic behavior. The lock-based approach is simpler to implement and maintain than the hybrid approach, and provides sufficient performance for the specified requirements.

decisions.decision: Deploy regional server clusters with global load balancing
decisions.alternatives_considered: Single global cluster, centralized processing, hybrid cloud approach
decisions.trade_offs: Regional deployment increases operational complexity but reduces latency for players worldwide
decisions.rationale: The sub-100ms latency requirement cannot be met with a single centralized server. Geographic distribution using regional clusters ensures that players connect to servers within their network proximity while maintaining overall system scalability and cost efficiency.

decisions.alternatives_considered: Stateless matchmaker, distributed consensus protocols, event sourcing, hybrid approach
decisions.trade_offs: Purely stateful approach reduces complexity and eliminates potential consistency issues
decisions.rationale: The system must support 50,000 concurrent matches at peak traffic while maintaining 99.95% availability. A purely stateful approach using direct database access provides the necessary simplicity and reliability without introducing single points of failure or complex caching layers.
